title: Linked lists
summary: Walk the list with a few named pointers and relink nodes in place. A dummy node in front removes the special case for the head.
idea: A node only knows its next node, so every change is a pointer rewrite. Name each pointer, change next in the right order, and you never lose the rest of the list.

signals.see: The input is a head node, and each node has val and next.
signals.think: Walk with a pointer. To change the list, rewrite next fields instead of copying values into an array.

signals.see: The head itself might be removed or replaced.
signals.think: Put a dummy node in front. Return dummy.next, and the head needs no special case.

signals.see: You must find the middle, a cycle, or the k-th node from the end in one pass.
signals.think: Use two pointers moving at different speeds or with a gap. See Fast & slow pointers.

signals.see: You must reverse the whole list or part of it without extra space.
signals.think: Keep prev, curr and next, and flip one arrow at a time. See In-place reversal.

phrasings: Remove every song by a given artist from a playlist stored as a linked list.
Merge two sorted chains of train carriages into one sorted chain.
Insert a new reading into a sorted linked list of sensor values.

picture.title: Relink, do not copy
picture.alt: On the left, the list is copied into an array, changed, and rebuilt, which uses O(n) extra space. On the right, a dummy node points at the head and a prev pointer walks the list, rewriting next to skip or insert nodes in place.
picture.caption: The dummy node means removing the head is just another skip.

before.label: Copy to an array and rebuild

after.label: Pattern: dummy node and a prev pointer

code.py:
def drop_value(head, val):
    dummy = {'val': 0, 'next': head}  #@init
    prev = dummy
    while prev['next']:  #@loop
        if prev['next']['val'] == val: prev['next'] = prev['next']['next']  #@drop
        else: prev = prev['next']  #@keep
    return dummy['next']  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 10 list values between -99 and 99, separated by commas (leave it empty for an empty list). The value to remove is between -99 and 99.

oneLiner: dummy → head; prev = dummy; skip with prev.next = prev.next.next, else step; return dummy.next

exercise.prompt: head is a linked list sorted from smallest to largest (it may be empty). Insert a new node with value val so the list stays sorted, and return the head. Nodes are { val, next } objects (dicts in Python). The starter walks from the head, so it breaks when the list is empty or val belongs first. Use a dummy node.
hints: If val belongs before the head, there is no node before it to link from. A dummy node in front gives you one.
Start prev at the dummy, walk while prev.next.val < val, link the new node after prev, and return dummy.next.

complexity.why: One walk visits each node once. Relinking reuses the existing nodes, so only a few pointers and one dummy node are extra.

mistakes: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it.
Moving prev forward right after removing a node, which skips the next node without checking it.
Special-casing the head with extra ifs instead of using a dummy node.
Reading node.next.val without checking that node.next exists.
Copying values into an array when the question asks for O(1) extra space.

quiz.question: Why put a dummy node in front of the head?
choices: Every real node, including the head, then has a node before it
quiz.explain: Removing or inserting needs the node before. The dummy gives the head one, so there is no special case. Return dummy.next.

quiz.question: You remove prev.next. Should prev move forward in the same step?
choices: No: the new prev.next has not been checked yet
Only at the end of the list
quiz.explain: After the skip, prev.next is a new node. Move prev only when you keep a node.

quiz.question: You must reverse a list in place. What do you save before flipping curr.next?
choices: curr.next, so the rest of the list is not lost
quiz.explain: Once curr.next points backwards, the old next node is unreachable unless you saved it first.

interviewTip: Draw three or four boxes with arrows and update them as you code. Interviewers like seeing each pointer change checked on the drawing, especially at the head and the tail.
